transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-28
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO - Nova Finance), Maya Patel (Head of ML), Diego Rivera (Infra)

Summary: quick scoping for POC to decide deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Covered success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plan, timeline, security requirements and decision criteria.

[00:00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick intros round and then jump into current workload, success criteria and how we usual run POCs for hosted/dedicated/private.

[00:00:18] Liam O'Connor: Hi Alex, thanks. I'm Liam, CTO. We've got Maya and Diego here. We're evaluating Redwood for transaction anomaly detection and automated customer support summarization, both high-sensitivity.

[00:00:32] Maya Patel: Hi. From ML, main focus is latency for real-time scoring (sub 200ms p95 ideally) and throughput for nightly batch embeddings. Also model fidelity on fraud detection prompts.

[00:00:45] Diego Rivera: Diego, infra. I'm worried about network egress, VPC requirements, and key management. We have strict controls, SOC2 type II, and some EU data residency needs.

[00:01:00] Alex Chen: Great, that aligns with what we usually see. Priya, can you outline the POC flow and benchmarks we propose?

[00:01:10] Priya Singh: Sure. Typical POC is 4 steps: 1) collect representative workload and success criteria, 2) run baseline benches on Hosted to validate perf/cost, 3) spin dedicated capacity to test isolation and autoscale, and 4) if required, validate Private (VPC/on-prem) for security/residency. For benchmarks we capture p50/p95/p99 latencies, throughput (reqs per second), token cost, and quality metrics (F1/precision@k for fraud models, or ROUGE for summarization).

[00:01:45] Maya Patel: For fraud scoring, our current baseline is about 150 RPS at peak, average seq length ~120 tokens, and we need p95 under 200ms for the low-latency path. For batching jobs (embeddings) it's around 2 million rows nightly, that's throughput oriented. Does Redwood support mixed workloads?

[00:02:05] Priya Singh: Yes, we see mixed patterns a lot. We can route by policy: keep a low-latency pool for scoring and a batch pool for embeddings. For Hosted we can prioritize, for Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools to guarantee throughput. For Private we can deploy similar pools inside your VPC.

[00:02:24] Diego Rivera: On Private, our questions: does Redwood support customer-managed KMS and HSM, and how is network set up for on-prem? We have no direct internet egress for PCI workloads.

[00:02:36] Priya Singh: We support customer KMS integration and can do private deployments with no public egress; that would be a Private deployment with an air-gapped or VPC-connected control plane depending on your requirements. We'll share the architecture doc.

[00:02:50] Liam O'Connor: Cost is a big factor. Hosted sounds easiest, but worried about per-token costs at scale. How does cost compare hosted vs dedicated? Ballpark numbers?

[00:03:03] Alex Chen: Ballpark: Hosted is easiest to start and lowest upfront; unit cost typically higher. Dedicated reduces per-token cost via reserved GPU capacity and optimizations like batching/quantization. Private has the highest setup cost but can have competitive unit cost at scale while meeting compliance. We'll send the pricing sheet.

[00:03:20] Maya Patel: What about model variants? We want to test both a smaller quantized model for scoring and a larger instruct model for summaries. Can we run both in the same POC?

[00:03:31] Priya Singh: Absolutely. We recommend running both: 1) a 4-bit quantized LlamaX variant for scoring (lower latency/cost) and 2) a 16-bit instruct model for summaries. Benchmarks will show trade-offs (latency vs quality).

[00:03:47] Diego Rivera: Are there known latency numbers for the quantized variant on dedicated infra?

[00:03:52] Priya Singh: Example numbers depend on GPU type and batch config; for A100-class dedicated pools, we often see p95 under 120-160ms at modest sequence lengths for quantized models, but we'll run your exact workload.

[00:04:05] Liam O'Connor: Timeline — how long does a POC take? We ideally want a decision within 6 weeks.

[00:04:13] Alex Chen: Typical POC length is 3-6 weeks. Week 1: data/workload collection and test plan. Week 2: hosted baseline runs and initial quality checks. Week 3: dedicated capacity setup and stress tests. Week 4: optional private deployment validation or deeper security review. We can compress if you provide logs quickly and prioritize hosted/dedicated first.

[00:04:33] Maya Patel: Success criteria we'd use: 1) p95 latency <200ms for scoring on production-like traffic, 2) identical or better detection F1 vs current model, 3) token unit cost within 30% of target, 4) security signoff for data handling.

[00:04:48] Priya Singh: That's clear and mapable to tests. We'll instrument the harness to report p50/p95/p99, cost per 1M tokens, and the evaluation metrics you listed.

[00:04:58] Diego Rivera: On security docs, we need SOC2, ISO, pen test summaries and the network architecture for Private deployment. Alex, can you send that?

[00:05:06] Alex Chen: Yep, I'll send the security package and SOC2 report link after the call.

[00:05:12] Liam O'Connor: One other blocker: data residency. Some customer PII must stay in EU. Can hosted satisfy that?

[00:05:18] Priya Singh: Hosted can run in EU regions; we maintain regional data residency options. If you need full isolation and customer control, Private is more appropriate. We'll confirm data retention and audit log retention settings for the hosted option.

[00:05:34] Maya Patel: For benchmarking, what do you need from us?

[00:05:38] Priya Singh: Representative request traces, RPS spike profile, sequence length histogram, and a subset of labeled examples for quality evals. Diego will send infra constraints and whether we can run network tests.

[00:05:50] Diego Rivera: I can extract logs and an anonymized sample. I'll include our peak RPS windows and some SLOs from our current infra.

[00:05:58] Alex Chen: Great. We'll then run a hosted baseline (3 days of runs), then if that looks good spin dedicated capacity for 2-3 days of stress tests, and optionally schedule a Private architecture review.

[00:06:10] Liam O'Connor: Decision criteria recap: if hosted meets p95 latency and cost goals and passes security checks, we prefer hosted to move faster. If not, and cost/latency need improvement, we go dedicated. Private is reserved for hard compliance/data residency needs or where on-prem is mandated.

[00:06:24] Priya Singh: Yep that's the standard decision tree. We'll also include fallback policies for graceful degradation (route to a smaller model if capacity constrained).

[00:06:34] Alex Chen: Alright let's wrap. Recap of next steps and action items: Redwood to send pricing and security docs, Redwood to share benchmark plan and harness, Nova to provide workload logs and labeled eval set, schedule benchmark week of 2025-02-10.

[00:06:47] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[00:06:50] Maya Patel: Thanks, talk soon.

[00:06:52] Diego Rivera: Thanks.

End of transcript.
